extracted_relationships.sentence: My father's father Israel Gonopolskiy was born in the late 1860s in the village of Petroverovka, Kherson province.
The name of my grandmother on my father's side was Mariam Gonopolskaya. She was born in Petroverovka in 1876.
By the late 1920s, when agricultural cooperatives were organized in villages, my grandfather and his wife moved to their children in Odessa.
My grandfather died in 1934, when my parents and I were absent, in Odessa.
During the Great Patriotic War my grandmother was in evacuation in Penza and then Kustanai with her younger daughter Dora's family.
They returned to Odessa from evacuation in 1944.
My father's older sister Hanna was born in 1899.
They moved to Odessa and lived in a big 25 square meter room in a communal apartment in Tiraspolskaya Street in the center of town.
Hanna worked at the shoe factory as a worker.
Her son Ilia was born in 1926.
During the war Hanna and her son were in evacuation in Kustanai with us.
In 1943 Ilia was recruited to the army, finished an aviation school of gunners/radio operators and was at the front.
Aunt Hanna's husband perished at the front during the Great Patriotic War.
Hanna returned to Odessa from evacuation in 1944 and worked at the same factory.
Ilia worked at a butchery in Odessa after the war.
He got married to a Jewish girl.
Their only daughter Rita was born in the 1950s.
Rita graduated from the Conservatory and played in the Odessa Opera orchestra.
She emigrated to the US in the 1990s.
Ilia died in 2000.
My father's sister Riva was born in 1903.
She went to study in Kiev to become an astronomer.
My father's brother Izia was born in 1906.
He moved to Odessa in the 1920s.
Izia married a Jewish girl, Rosa, but they didn't have children.
In the middle of the 1930s he was recruited to the army.
Izia perished at the front in 1943.
My father's sister Dora was born in 1910.
She moved to Odessa after my father.
My father managed to help her get employment at the buttery.
Dora got married to a Jew, Efim Mezhysko.
Her husband was an officer in the Red Army.
In 1938 their son Senia was born.
At the beginning of the war Dora's husband was wounded.
He was taken to a hospital in Odessa.
Then Dora, her son and Grandmother Mariam left Odessa escorting Dora's husband to the rear.
They were in Penza where Dora's husband was in hospital.
After he recovered he returned to the front and my aunt, her son and my grandmother joined us in Kustanai.
They returned to Odessa after it was liberated.
Dora's husband perished at the front.
After the war Dora worked at the bakery factory and then in the trade business.
Aunt Dora died in 1991.
Dora's son Senia Mezhysko worked as a docker in Odessa port.
In the late 1990s he emigrated to the US with his wife Nonna, a Jewess, his son Mikhail and his son's family.
My father's youngest brother Lyonia was born in 1913.
He served in the army in the middle of the 1930s.
He went to the front in the rank of lieutenant when the war began and perished at the end of 1941.
My father Nusia Gonopolskiy was born in Petroverovka in 1901.
My grandfather on my mother's side Simkha Weiser was born in Petroverovka in the 1860s.
My grandfather died in Petroverovka in the 1920s.
The name of my grandmother on my mother's side was Tsylia Weiser. She was born in Petroverovka in the late 1870s.
My grandmother lived in Petroverovka until 1935.
My mother's oldest brother Tsalia Weiser was born around 1899.
He lived in Odessa at the time I remember him.
Uncle Tsalia died of cancer shortly before the war.
His daughter Polia was born in 1919.
Before the Great Patriotic War she worked at the telephone exchange center.
During the war she was evacuated to Tashkent.
Afterwards she returned to Odessa and worked at the same place as before.
She married Misha Krutyansky, a Jew.
Polia died in 1986.
My mother's brother Yasha Weiser was born in 1901.
He was married to a Jewish girl, Zhenia.
Their son Lyova, born in 1921, graduated from the Faculty of Physics and Mathematics at Odessa University.
Uncle Yasha and Lyova were recruited to the army at the very beginning of the Great Patriotic War.
Zhenia perished in Odessa during the occupation.
After the war Yasha married Rosa, the widow of his younger brother Moisey, and moved to the town of Rustavi in the Caucasus.
Uncle Yasha died in the middle of the 1980s.
My mother's third brother Moisey Weiser was born in 1906.
Uncle Moisey worked at the confectionary factory.
Uncle Moisey died of cancer before the war.
His daughters live in Israel.
My mother's younger sister Mara Weiser was born in 1908.
She got married and lived in the same building as Uncle Moisey in Frantz Mering Street in Odessa.
During the occupation Mara and her daughter stayed in Odessa.
They perished in the ghetto.
My mother Rosa Weiser was born in Petroverovka in 1903.
They had a traditional Jewish wedding in the late 1920s.
The newly-weds moved to Odessa.
My father went to work at the buttery.
I was born on 17th November 1927.
I remember when in 1933 my father came home and said that all communists were sent to villages to help collective farmers since they were having a hard time.
He left and in some time my mother and I joined him in the village of Grossulovo, Odessa region.
In the fall of 1934 after harvesting was over we returned to the town.
I started school in 1936.
I studied in a Ukrainian school.
I was also fond of modeling and attended a modeling club at the Town House of Pioneers.
On 23rd June 1941 - the second day of the war - we saw German planes for the first time.
Germans began to bomb Odessa about a month after the war began.
When Privoz market was set on fire we moved into Uncle Moisey's apartment in the center of the town.
His family moved to some relatives in the neighborhood of Fontanka.
The hardest time was when Germans occupied Beliaevka where there was a water supply facility.
My father was in a fighting battalion that fought against German forces that landed in the rear.
All I know is that my father was in the Primorskaya army defending Odessa.
On 28th September we got tickets enabling us to board a ship.
My father took us there along with his sister Hanna and her son Ilia on a military truck.
Our ship left Odessa in the evening.
In two days we reached Novorossiysk where we were accommodated in some storage facility.
Later we left in eastern direction by train.
In the fall of 1941 we arrived in the town of Kustanai in Kazakhstan.
I went to the 7th grade at school in Kustanai.
I finished the 7th grade at the age of 15.
I went to work as an assistant worker at the woodworking facility.
When Odessa was liberated in April 1944 my mother wrote to the Volkovs, our neighbor tenants.
My mother left for Odessa.
She returned to our apartment in Privoznaya Street.
My father didn't return from the front and we didn't receive any notification about him.
They were near Sevastopol and after Sevastopol was left to the Germans they relocated to Novorossiysk.
Shortly afterwards my mother received the notification that my father was missing.
In the 1970s I went to the chief military archive in Podolsk where I got confirmation that my father had perished near Novorossiysk.
In the army I continued serving as an aviation mechanic in the same unit where I had worked as a civilian.
In 1945 our military unit relocated to Novosibirsk.
I demobilized in the rank of master sergeant in 1952.
I arrived in Odessa in 1952.
I went to work at Kirov machine tool plant.
In 1953 I entered the evening department at Leningrad Industrial Institute.
I met my future wife Ella Gellerman at the institute in 1953.
She was born in Kharkov in 1933.
Her family lived in Kharkov before the war.
Her father Jacob Gellerman was recruited to the army in the first days of the war.
He perished near Leningrad in 1943.
Her mother Bella Gellerman and Ella were in evacuation in Sterlitamak, Bashkiria.
Ella's sister Ania, born in Sterlitamak at the end of 1941, never saw her father.
Ania graduated from a technical college in Odessa and worked at the same plant as me.
In 1960 she married Valentin Bekker, a Jew, her school mate.
Ella's mother worked at the machine tool plant.
The plant relocated to Odessa in 1944.
Ella's family moved to Odessa with the plant.
They received a small room in a communal apartment.
Ella went to study at the flour milling college after finishing lower secondary school.
After finishing college she completed her two-year job assignment in Odessa region.
After that she got employment at the bakery in Odessa where she was a production engineer.
Later she entered the machine building faculty of Odessa Polytechnic College.
We got married in 1956.
In 1957 the plant constructed its first apartment building for employees where we received a room in a communal apartment.
We lived there for 15 years until 1972.
We graduated from the institute in 1959.
Our son was born on 1st April 1960.
My mother died in 1962.
We buried her in the Jewish cemetery.
Upon graduation I was promoted to the engineer's position at the design office.
Later I became head of the design department that designed accessories for machine units.
Later I became deputy chief engineer for export operations and sometimes I traveled abroad.
In 1972 we moved to another neighborhood where the plant constructed another apartment building.
We received a two-bedroom apartment and my son got a room of his own.
In this same apartment building my wife's mother received a one-bedroom apartment.
My son Natan finished school in 1977 and entered the Mechanic Faculty of Polytechnic College.
Upon graduation he worked at the Research Institute of Machine and Automatic Units.

extracted_relationships.sentence: He entered the post-graduate school in the Machine Building Institute in Moscow.
He met his wife Evgenia Trofimova at the sailing club.
Their son Roman, my grandson, was born in 1987.
My wife worked at SKB-3, a special design office.
She climbed up the ladder until she reached the position of 1st grade designer.
Ella died in a bus accident in 2000 on her way back home from Germany where she was visiting her mother and younger sister.
We buried her in accordance with the Jewish tradition in the Jewish cemetery in Odessa.
